title: A Root Grows by Cells Times Length

scenes.tts: A tree keeps adding roots, branches and leaves for as long as it lives. Take the root of a flowering plant. It gets longer. Does it make more cells, or do its cells get longer? Behind the tip, under a protective root cap, you can see three zones.
scenes.visual: A schematic cell file with a root cap; a long arrow shows it lengthening; two question chips, more cells and longer cells; three numbered braces.
scenes.narration: A tree keeps adding roots, branches and leaves for as long as it lives. Take the root of a flowering plant. It gets longer. Does it make more cells, or do its cells get longer? Behind the tip, under a protective root cap, you can see three zones.

scenes.tts: In the zone of division, small cells divide. In the zone of elongation, they stop dividing and lengthen many times over, as water fills their vacuoles. In the zone of maturation, they become their final types, and root hairs appear on the epidermis.
scenes.visual: The same strip: division zone cells split, elongation zone vacuoles fill, maturation zone gains root hairs; each zone gets its colour and name.
scenes.narration: In the zone of division, small cells divide. In the zone of elongation, they stop dividing and lengthen many times over, as water fills their vacuoles. In the zone of maturation, they become their final types, and root hairs appear on the epidermis.

scenes.tts: So growth has two parts. Division makes the cells. Elongation sets their length. Assume the root is at steady state, with every cell file alike. Then root growth rate equals the rate of new cells per file, times the final cell length. The numbers that follow are illustrative. They are not from a measured species.
scenes.caption: So growth has two parts. Division makes the cells. Elongation sets their length. Assume the root is at steady state, with every cell file alike. Then root growth rate equals the rate of new cells per file, times the final cell length. The numbers that follow are illustrative. They are not from a measured species.
scenes.visual: The strip shrinks to the bottom; the rule appears with the first term in the division colour and the second in the elongation colour, each tied to its zone by an arrow.
scenes.narration: So growth has two parts. Division makes the cells. Elongation sets their length. Assume the root is at steady state, with every cell file alike. Then root growth rate equals the rate of new cells per file, times the final cell length. The numbers that follow are illustrative. They are not from a measured species.

scenes.tts: Take one file of cells. It delivers one new cell per hour from the meristem. Each cell leaves the meristem fifteen micrometres long, and matures at three hundred micrometres. One cell per hour times three hundred micrometres is three hundred micrometres per hour. Over twenty four hours, that is seven point two millimetres per day.
scenes.caption: Take one file of cells. It delivers 1 new cell per hour from the meristem. Each cell leaves the meristem 15 µm long, and matures at 300 µm. 1 cell per hour times 300 µm is 300 µm per hour. Over 24 hours, that is 7.2 mm per day.
scenes.visual: One cell file: each hour a tiny new cell appears behind the root cap and lengthens, pushing the tip forward; the arithmetic appears beneath and the first bar is drawn.
scenes.narration: Take one file of cells. It delivers 1 new cell per hour from the meristem. Each cell leaves the meristem 15 µm long, and matures at 300 µm. 1 cell per hour times 300 µm is 300 µm per hour. Over 24 hours, that is 7.2 mm per day.

scenes.tts: Now block elongation, and leave division alone. Division still delivers one new cell per hour. But the cells stay fifteen micrometres long. One times fifteen is fifteen micrometres per hour. That is zero point three six millimetres per day, one twentieth of normal. So elongation supplies most of the length.
scenes.caption: Now block elongation, and leave division alone. Division still delivers one new cell per hour. But the cells stay 15 µm long. 1 times 15 is 15 µm per hour. That is 0.36 mm per day, one twentieth of normal. So elongation supplies most of the length.
scenes.visual: Elongation is struck out; new cells stay tiny and the tip barely moves; the arithmetic and a second, very short bar appear.
scenes.narration: Now block elongation, and leave division alone. Division still delivers one new cell per hour. But the cells stay 15 µm long. 1 times 15 is 15 µm per hour. That is 0.36 mm per day, one twentieth of normal. So elongation supplies most of the length.

scenes.tts: Instead, halve division, and keep elongation normal. Half a cell per hour times three hundred micrometres is one hundred fifty micrometres per hour. That is three point six millimetres per day, half of normal. A change in growth can come from either part, or from both. Keep the rule. Root growth rate equals new cells per hour times final cell length.
scenes.caption: Instead, halve division, and keep elongation normal. Half a cell per hour times 300 µm is 150 µm per hour. That is 3.6 mm per day, half of normal. A change in growth can come from either part, or from both. Keep the rule. Root growth rate equals new cells per hour times final cell length.
scenes.visual: Division is halved: a new cell appears every second hour; third bar is drawn; the rule is restated with all three bars in view.
